title: Quantum-Correlation-Based Multi-Emitter Localization in Information-Limited Regimes via Learned Inference
authors: Sanket K. Tripathy, Simeon I. Bogdanov
abstract: Quantum correlation measurements have emerged as a powerful tool for localizing multiple emitters with subwavelength separation. Multi-emitter localization consists of two distinct tasks: identifying the emitter count $N$ and estimating their positions $\left\{x^{i}\right\}$. Existing fit-and-select frameworks fit the measured intensity and autocorrelation data using several models corresponding to different values of $N$ and then select the best-supported model. This procedure lets errors from the multi-parameter optimization of emitter positions propagate into the choice of model, degrading performance under photon-limited and high-background conditions. We propose a method that directly infers the emitter count and positions from the multimodal data via learned inference. Learned inference improves both the emitter-counting accuracy and localization precision compared to the fit-and-select method. It achieves more than tenfold improvement in precision and requires up to five times fewer photons to achieve practically meaningful localization with the largest gains observed under low photon counts, strong background, narrowly spaced emitter configurations, and spatially truncated data. This photon-efficient quantum-assisted localization framework offers a promising route toward real-time biological imaging and single-particle tracking in densely labeled samples.
summary: This paper introduces a machine learning approach to overcome limitations in localizing multiple quantum emitters using quantum correlation measurements. By employing a two-stage neural network pipeline, the method accurately determines both the number and positions of emitters, showing substantial performance gains over traditional fitting techniques, particularly when photon counts are low.
main_problem: The core problem is accurately performing multi-emitter localization, which requires simultaneously determining the number of emitters ($N$) and estimating their individual positions ($\{x_i\}$) from quantum correlation measurements.
main_result: The proposed learned inference framework significantly outperforms traditional fit-and-select methods, achieving $>10	imes$ improvement in localization precision and requiring up to $5	imes$ fewer photons, especially in low-photon or high-background regimes.
method: The authors propose a two-stage deep learning pipeline: a Classification-NN to infer $N$ from intensity and correlation data, followed by a Regression-NN to estimate positions conditioned on the inferred $N$.
model_or_system: The system involves single-photon emitters (SPEs) whose photoluminescence is measured using a Hanbury Brown–Twiss (HBT) interferometer, yielding spatially sampled intensity $I(x)$ and second-order correlation $g^{(2)}(x)$ data.
key_observables: Intensity $I(x)$, second-order correlation $g^{(2)}(x)$, Emitter Count ($N$), and Emitter Positions ($\{x_i\}$).
important_parameters: Photon budget ($n_{	ext{pulse}}$), Signal-to-Background Ratio (SBR), and minimum emitter separation.
main_assumptions: The traditional fit-and-select method suffers from model selection bias and error propagation from multi-parameter optimization, which the learned inference bypasses.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the measurement setup and the performance of the fit-and-select vs. learned inference approaches. Figure 2 demonstrates the failure modes of the fit-and-select method, showing counting accuracy degradation. Figure 3 details the dual-branch CNN architecture for both classification and regression tasks.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of existing fit-and-select methods. It then introduces the novel learned inference pipeline, detailing the architecture of the Classification-NN and the Regression-NN, and finally presents quantitative results demonstrating superior performance under various low-photon and high-background conditions.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics measurement theory with advanced machine learning, providing a robust computational tool for characterizing complex quantum light sources, which is highly relevant for quantum sensing and imaging.

The measured intensity, I(x), and second- order correlation, g(2)(x), are processed by separate convolutional feature-extraction branches. The resulting feature vectors are combined by an adaptive feature-fusion layer using photon-budget-dependent weighting and subsequently passed to a fully connected task-specific network. Figure 4. Emitter-counting accuracy as a function of emitter separation and photon budget. Results are shown for ground-truth emitter counts 𝑁GT = 2 and 𝑁GT = 3 (sections) and SBR = 2, 6 and 10 (columns). Within each section, the upper row shows results for the proposed Classification-NN, and the lower row shows results for the fit-and-select approach. Each heatmap shows emitter-counting accuracy as a function of the minimum ground-truth emitter separation and the photon budget 𝑛pulse, evaluated over Monte Carlo realizations on identical simulated datasets.

Figure 5: Position-estimation standard deviation as a function of emitter separation and photon budget. Results are shown for ground-truth emitter counts NGT = 2 and NGT = 3 (sections) and SBR 2, 6 and 10 (columns). Within each section, the upper row shows results for the proposed Regression-NN, and the lower row shows results for the existing fit-and-select approach. N is fixed to the ground-truth value for both approaches. Each heatmap shows the standard deviation of the position-estimation error as a function of the minimum ground- truth emitter separation and the number of excitation pulses, evaluated over independent Monte Carlo realizations on identical simulated datasets.
